The GRIMMER test (granularity-related inconsistency of means mapped to error repeats)

Source: R/grimmer.R
grimmer.Rd

grimmer() checks whether a reported mean and standard deviation of integer data are consistent with the reported sample size and the number of items averaged. It extends grim(): the mean must pass GRIM, and the SD must then be reachable from one of the integer sums that GRIM admits.

The function is vectorized, but grimmer_map() is more convenient for testing many cases.

Usage

grimmer(
  x,
  sd,
  n,
  digits_x,
  digits_sd,
  items_averaged,
  data_type,
  sd_meaning = c("sd_sample", "sd_pop", "sd_sample_or_pop", "se"),
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  symmetric = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

Numeric. The reported mean.

sd

Numeric. The reported standard deviation.

n

Integer. The reported sample size.

digits_x

Integer. The number of decimal places in x, including trailing zeros. There is no default, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4).

digits_sd

Integer. The number of decimal places in sd, including trailing zeros. There is no default, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4).

items_averaged

Integer. As in grim(), for x and sd.

data_type

String. As in grim(): "integer" or "continuous". No default. Continuous data can have any mean and any SD of 0 or more, but a single value only an SD of 0.

sd_meaning

String. What sd really is. "sd_sample" (the default) is the sample SD, which divides by n - 1; "sd_pop" is the population SD, which divides by n; "sd_sample_or_pop" accepts either; "se" is the standard error of the mean, the sample SD divided by sqrt(n), reported as if it were an SD. See Defaults and SD meaning in grimmer().

rounding

String. The rounding method assumed to have produced x. Default is "up_or_down", which accepts either direction; see Defaults in grim(). The others are "up_from_or_down_from", "ceiling_or_floor", "up", "down", "even", "up_from", "down_from", "ceiling", "floor", "trunc", "anti_trunc", "ties_up", "ties_down", "ties_away", "ties_zero", and "ties_even". See vignette("rounding-options", package = "roundwork").

threshold

Numeric. For rounding = "up_from", "down_from", or "up_from_or_down_from", the point within a step at which rounding switches direction, in tenths of a step. Default is 5. Ignored otherwise.

symmetric

Logical. If TRUE, negative numbers are rounded like their absolute values (-2.5 like 2.5) under "up", "down", and the "*_from" methods. Default is FALSE. Must not be TRUE with a "ties_*" rounding method, which already fixes the direction; see roundwork::reround().

Value

Logical. TRUE if x, sd, n, and items_averaged are consistent, FALSE if not, and NA if the case cannot be decided: if a value is infinite, if n or items_averaged is not a positive whole number, or if a missing value could decide the case either way. See vignette("technical-notes"), section Missing values, on which cases a missing value leaves open. A sample SD divides by n - 1, so under sd_meaning = "sd_sample" (the default) and "se", n must also be at least 2.

Details

x, sd, n, digits_x, digits_sd, items_averaged, and data_type are vectorized and recycled to a common length by the tidyverse rules. All other arguments must have length 1.

The implementation follows Allard's (2018) Analytic-GRIMMER algorithm, as does rsprite2::GRIMMER_test(), with a stricter first test: the sum of squares must be one that n whole numbers with the reconstructed sum can have. For n >= 5, this means at least the smallest such sum of squares; for smaller n, some larger ones are impossible, too. With this test, grimmer() is TRUE if and only if a sample of whole numbers has a mean and SD that would be reported as x and sd. The one exception is rounding = "even", or its synonym "ties_even", which takes a value on a rounding bound to round either way, as in roundwork::unround(), so it may also accept a value set that a sample only rounds to if ties are broken the other way. GRIMMER was first proposed by Anaya (2016).

For data on a bounded scale, such as a Likert scale, see the strait package. Its brimmest() decides exactly whether a mean and SD are possible within the bounds.

x and sd are limited to about 15 significant digits, and x with n and items_averaged as in grim(). Within these limits, grimmer() decides value sets of any size exactly, but refuses two kinds that no study reports: with n from 2 to 4, SDs above about 3e5 to 1e6 (divided by items_averaged), depending on n and sd_meaning; and value sets with more than a million candidate sums, which takes an n of more than a million.

Defaults

sd_meaning = "sd_sample" because the sample SD is what nearly all software reports by default: R's sd(), SPSS, Stata, SAS, Excel's STDEV() and STDEV.S(), and pandas' .std(). The main exception is NumPy, whose np.std() returns the population SD unless ddof = 1 is given; so does Python's statistics.pstdev(). If the data may have been analyzed that way, or an inconsistent value set has a small n, test it under "sd_pop" as well. See SD meaning.

The rounding defaults are explained in grim().

SD meaning

The sample and population SDs differ by a factor of sqrt(n / (n - 1)), which matters most at small n, where GRIMMER is most powerful. A population SD tested as a sample SD will often seem inconsistent, so sd_meaning lets you check whether a value set is consistent only under the other convention.

"sd_sample_or_pop" is TRUE if the value set is consistent as a sample SD or as a population SD, and FALSE if it is neither. A single value has no sample SD, so at n = 1, "sd_sample_or_pop" is the same as "sd_pop". The reason column of grimmer_map() names the convention a value set passed under, trying the sample SD first.

"sd_sample_or_pop" accepts more SDs than either convention alone, so it is not the default. It also judges each value set on its own, although a single study usually computed all its SDs the same way. To tell which convention fits a set of values, test them under "sd_sample" and "sd_pop" separately.

Some papers report a standard error as if it were an SD. "se" tests whether a value set is consistent under that premise. The SE was rounded, not the SD, so the SD may lie anywhere in the SE's rounding range times sqrt(n). This range is wide: from about n = 30 on, nearly every value set whose mean passes GRIM is consistent under "se". Such a result says little, and it is no evidence that an SE was reported.

"se" is the SE of this group's mean, computed from its own sample SD and n. Model-based SEs, such as those of estimated marginal means, or SEs based on a pooled variance, are not. A value set that is inconsistent under "se" may still have been reported with one of them.

References

Allard, A. (2018). Analytic-GRIMMER: a new way of testing the possibility of standard deviations. https://aurelienallard.netlify.app/post/anaytic-grimmer-possibility-standard-deviations/

Anaya, J. (2016). The GRIMMER test: A method for testing the validity of reported measures of variability. PeerJ Preprints. https://peerj.com/preprints/2400v1/

See also

grimmer_explain() to explain a result in plain words, grimmer_map() for data frames, and grimmer_values() for the means and SDs behind a consistent value set.

Examples

# A mean of 5.23 is not consistent with an SD of 2.55
# and a sample size of 35:
grimmer(
  x = 5.23,
  sd = 2.55,
  n = 35,
  digits_x = 2,
  digits_sd = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] FALSE

# However, mean and SD are consistent with a
# sample size of 31:
grimmer(
  x = 5.23,
  sd = 2.55,
  n = 31,
  digits_x = 2,
  digits_sd = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] TRUE

# For a scale composed of two items:
grimmer(
  x = 2.74,
  sd = 0.96,
  n = 63,
  digits_x = 2,
  digits_sd = 2,
  items_averaged = 2,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] TRUE
